title: Real Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP)
summary: Defines the Real Time Streaming Protocol, an application-level protocol for controlling the delivery of data with real-time properties such as audio and video. It acts like a remote control for streaming servers, supporting controlled, on-demand delivery. It was replaced by RFC 7826.

plainLanguage.summary: RTSP is the protocol a player uses to control a streaming server. The client asks what a stream contains, sets up the transport, starts playback, pauses, seeks and tears down. The audio and video themselves travel separately, so RTSP is a set of instructions rather than a data stream.

questions: how does real time streaming protocol work
subtitle: A network remote control for streaming servers: it starts, pauses, seeks and stops the media.

tldr.problem: A client that wants to play a live or stored audio or video stream needs a way to ask a server for it, to choose where the data should go, to start and stop it, and to jump around inside it.
tldr.mechanism: RTSP is an application-level control protocol with methods modelled on HTTP: DESCRIBE, SETUP, PLAY, PAUSE, TEARDOWN and others, each carrying a session identifier so the server can correlate requests with a stream.
tldr.outcome: RTSP controls the stream but does not carry it: the media itself travels out of band, usually over RTP. The document has been replaced by RFC 7826.

facts.label: State-changing methods
facts.value: SETUP, PLAY, RECORD, PAUSE and TEARDOWN

today: RFC 2326 was a Proposed Standard published in April 1998. It has been obsoleted by RFC 7826, which is the current specification of the Real Time Streaming Protocol.

sections.title: What RTSP Is For
sections.content:
The Real-Time Streaming Protocol establishes and controls either a single or several time-synchronized streams of continuous media such as audio and video. It does not typically deliver the continuous streams itself, although interleaving of the continuous media stream with the control stream is possible. In other words, RTSP acts as a network remote control for multimedia servers.

The set of streams to be controlled is defined by a presentation description, and this memorandum does not define a format for that description. There is no notion of an RTSP connection: instead, a server maintains a session labeled by an identifier, and an RTSP session is in no way tied to a transport-level connection such as a TCP connection. During a session the client may open and close many reliable transport connections to the server to issue RTSP requests, or it may use a connectionless transport protocol such as UDP.

The protocol supports three operations. The client can request a presentation description, by HTTP or some other method; if the presentation is being multicast the description contains the multicast addresses and ports to use, and if it is to be sent only to the client by unicast the client provides the destination for security reasons. A media server can be invited to join an existing conference, either to play back media into the presentation or to record all or a subset of it, which is useful for distributed teaching applications where several parties take turns pushing the remote control buttons. And for live presentations it is useful if the server can tell the client about additional media becoming available. RTSP requests may also be handled by proxies, tunnels and caches as in HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: RTSP is a remote control for media servers. It does not carry the media; it tells a server what to send, where to send it and when to stop.

sections.title: Protocol Properties and the Difference from HTTP
sections.content:
The protocol is intentionally similar in syntax and operation to HTTP/1.1, so that extension mechanisms to HTTP can in most cases also be added to RTSP. However, RTSP differs in a number of important aspects. It introduces a number of new methods and has a different protocol identifier. An RTSP server needs to maintain state by default in almost all cases, as opposed to the stateless nature of HTTP. Both an RTSP server and client can issue requests. Data is carried out-of-band by a different protocol. RTSP is defined to use ISO 10646 (UTF-8) rather than ISO 8859-1. And the Request-URI always contains the absolute URI, where HTTP/1.1 carries only the absolute path in the request and puts the host name in a separate header field, which makes virtual hosting easier.

The RFC lists the properties of the protocol. RTSP is extendable, since new methods and parameters can be easily added. It is easy to parse, since RTSP can be parsed by standard HTTP or MIME parsers. It is secure, because it re-uses web security mechanisms: all HTTP authentication mechanisms such as basic and digest authentication are directly applicable, and transport or network layer security mechanisms may also be reused. It is transport-independent, using an unreliable datagram protocol, a reliable datagram protocol, or a reliable stream protocol such as TCP, as it implements application-level reliability.

It is multi-server capable, so each media stream within a presentation can reside on a different server and the client automatically establishes several concurrent control sessions with them, with media synchronization performed at the transport level. It can control recording as well as playback devices. Stream control is divorced from conference initiation, so SIP or H.323 may be used to invite a server to a conference. It supports frame-level accuracy through SMPTE time stamps to allow remote digital editing. It is presentation description neutral, though the description must contain at least one RTSP URI. And it is proxy and firewall friendly, although a firewall may need to understand the SETUP method to open a hole for the UDP media stream.
sections.plainLanguage: RTSP borrows HTTP's shape, which makes authentication and proxying easy to reuse, but it keeps server state, lets the server send requests too, and puts the media on a different connection.

sections.title: Overall Operation
sections.content:
Each presentation and media stream may be identified by an RTSP URL. The overall presentation and the properties of the media it is made up of are defined by a presentation description file, the format of which is outside the scope of this specification. The file may be obtained by the client using HTTP or other means such as email, and may not necessarily be stored on the media server.

The presentation description file contains a description of the media streams making up the presentation, including their encodings, language and other parameters that enable the client to choose the most appropriate combination of media. Each media stream that is individually controllable by RTSP is identified by an RTSP URL, which points to the media server handling that stream and names the stream stored on that server. Several media streams can be located on different servers; for example, audio and video streams can be split across servers for load sharing. The description also enumerates which transport methods the server is capable of.

The URLs use the rtsp and rtspu schemes. The scheme rtsp requires that commands are issued via a reliable protocol, within the Internet TCP, while rtspu identifies an unreliable protocol, within the Internet UDP. If the port is empty or not given, port 554 is assumed. A URL such as rtsp://media.example.com:554/twister/audiotrack identifies the audio stream within the presentation twister, while rtsp://media.example.com:554/twister identifies the presentation itself, which may be composed of audio and video streams.

Besides the media parameters, the network destination address and port need to be determined. In unicast the media is transmitted to the source of the RTSP request, with the port number chosen by the client, or on the same reliable stream as RTSP. In multicast with the server choosing the address, the media server picks the multicast address and port, which is the typical case for a live or near-media-on-demand transmission. In multicast with the client choosing, the address, port and encryption key are given by the conference description, established by means outside the scope of this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A description file lists the streams in a presentation and gives each one an address of the form rtsp://host:port/path. The server then needs to know where to send the media: back to the client, or to a multicast group.

sections.title: The Methods
sections.content:
OPTIONS may be issued at any time, for example if the client is about to try a nonstandard request. It does not influence server state, and the server lists the methods it supports using the Public response header.

DESCRIBE retrieves the description of a presentation or media object identified by the request URL. It may use the Accept header to specify the description formats the client understands, and the reply-response pair constitutes the media initialization phase of RTSP. The DESCRIBE response MUST contain all media initialization information for the resources it describes, and servers SHOULD NOT use it as a means of media indirection.

ANNOUNCE serves two purposes: sent from client to server it posts the description of a presentation or media object, and sent from server to client it updates the session description in real time. If a new media stream is added to a presentation, the whole presentation description should be sent again rather than just the additional components, so that components can be deleted.

SETUP for a URI specifies the transport mechanism to be used for the streamed media. A client can issue a SETUP request for a stream that is already playing to change transport parameters, which a server MAY allow; if it does not allow this it MUST respond with error 455 Method Not Valid In This State. Because SETUP includes all transport initialization information, firewalls and other intermediate devices are spared the more arduous task of parsing the DESCRIBE response. The server generates session identifiers in response to SETUP requests, and if a SETUP request includes a session identifier the server MUST bundle it into the existing session or return error 459.

PLAY tells the server to start sending data via the mechanism specified in SETUP. A client MUST NOT issue a PLAY request until any outstanding SETUP requests have been acknowledged as successful. The PLAY request positions the normal play time to the beginning of the range specified and delivers stream data until the end of the range is reached. PLAY requests may be pipelined: a server MUST queue PLAY requests to be executed in order, so a PLAY request arriving while a previous one is still active is delayed until the first has been completed, which allows precise editing.

PAUSE temporarily halts a stream without freeing server resources, and TEARDOWN frees the resources associated with the stream, after which the RTSP session ceases to exist on the server. GET_PARAMETER and SET_PARAMETER retrieve and set stream parameters, REDIRECT asks the client to go to another server, and RECORD starts a recording session. Because not all media servers have the same functionality, a server may support only playback and have no need for RECORD, may not support seeking, or may not support GET_PARAMETER and SET_PARAMETER.
sections.plainLanguage: The methods mirror what a person does with a remote control: ask what is available, set up the connection, play, pause, adjust and stop. The server replies with a status code and, where relevant, a session identifier to use on later requests.

sections.title: Sessions and State
sections.content:
RTSP controls a stream which may be sent via a separate protocol, independent of the control channel. For example, RTSP control may occur on a TCP connection while the data flows via UDP, so data delivery continues even if no RTSP requests are received by the media server. Also, during its lifetime a single media stream may be controlled by RTSP requests issued sequentially on different TCP connections. The server therefore needs to maintain session state to be able to correlate RTSP requests with a stream.

Many methods in RTSP do not contribute to state. The following play a central role in defining the allocation and usage of stream resources: SETUP causes the server to allocate resources for a stream and start an RTSP session; PLAY and RECORD start data transmission on a stream allocated via SETUP; PAUSE temporarily halts a stream without freeing server resources; and TEARDOWN frees the resources associated with the stream, so that the RTSP session ceases to exist on the server. These methods use the Session header field to identify the RTSP session whose state is being manipulated, and the server generates session identifiers in response to SETUP requests.

Appendix A gives the client and server state machines. State is defined on a per object basis, where an object is uniquely identified by the stream URL and the RTSP session identifier. The client can be in Init, which means SETUP has been sent and the reply is awaited, Ready, Playing or Recording. A status code of 3xx moves the client to Init, a 4xx yields no change in state, and the requests OPTIONS, ANNOUNCE, DESCRIBE, GET_PARAMETER and SET_PARAMETER have no effect on state at all. The server can be in Init, Ready, Playing or Recording, and if it is in Playing or Recording and in unicast mode it MAY revert to Init and tear down the session if it has not received wellness information, such as RTCP reports or RTSP commands, from the client for a defined interval, with a default of one minute.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the media runs on its own connection, the server has to remember which requests belong to which stream. The Session header carries the number that does that, and the appendix lists the four states each side can be in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because of the similarity in syntax and usage between RTSP servers and HTTP servers, the security considerations of HTTP apply. RTSP and HTTP share common authentication schemes and should follow the same prescriptions. Servers should be equally careful in protecting the contents of their logs, thus protecting the privacy of the users of the servers. There is no reason to believe that information transferred via RTSP may be any less sensitive than that normally transmitted via HTTP. Though RTSP URLs are opaque handles that do not necessarily have file system semantics, it is anticipated that many implementations will translate portions of the request URLs directly to file system calls, so file systems SHOULD follow the HTTP precautions, such as checking for .. in path components.

Four considerations are added for RTSP. The protocol offers the opportunity for a remote-controlled denial-of-service attack: an attacker may initiate traffic flows to one or more IP addresses by specifying them as the destination in SETUP requests. An RTSP server SHOULD only allow client-specified destinations for RTSP-initiated traffic flows if the server has verified the client's identity, preferably with digest authentication or stronger. Session hijacking is possible because there is no relation between a transport layer connection and an RTSP session, so the server SHOULD use a large, random and non-sequential session identifier. Servers SHOULD implement both basic and digest authentication, and in environments requiring tighter security the RTSP control stream may be encrypted. Finally, servers SHOULD return error code 403 Forbidden upon receiving a single instance of behavior which is deemed a security risk, and MAY arbitrarily disconnect and ignore further requests from clients deemed to be in violation of local security policy.
sections.plainLanguage: RTSP inherits HTTP's security rules and adds two of its own: a client can ask the server to send media to an address of its choosing, which can be abused, and a client can guess someone else's session number.

messages.label: OPTIONS
messages.note: Asks which methods the server supports. Does not change state.

messages.label: DESCRIBE
messages.note: Returns the presentation description and all media initialization information.

messages.label: SETUP
messages.note: Negotiates the transport. The server replies with a Session identifier.

messages.label: PLAY
messages.note: Starts sending the data, optionally from a given range.

messages.label: PAUSE
messages.note: Halts the stream but keeps the resources.

messages.label: TEARDOWN
messages.note: Releases the resources and ends the session.
